doc.title: Charles Calello interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 21, 2025

title: A changing industry, Hugo Winterhalter, and moving to Florida
summary: He saw Winterhalter lose work when styles changed, feared the same, then found arranging work for the Pops after moving to Florida in 1992.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Yeah. It was sort of – I think you know taking into consideration, you mentioned something very, very early on about how rewarding it was to write arrangements. But there was also a – it was – I recognized that my career would probably only last maybe twenty, thirty years. And I had an office in the ‘60s at Al Gallico’s office. You may not know who Al Gallico was but he was a publisher and he published “Stand By Your Man” and he was basically Billy – oh I can’t remember his name now. But every day Hugo Winterhalter used to come in and sit down in his office and hang out with Al. Now I grew up listening to Hugo Winterhalter who was a key arranger on RCA Victor. But while I was making all these records and I was doing record after record, he didn’t have work. And the reason why he didn’t have work, the music style had changed. And as it changed they didn’t have the opportunity to make the change because they were stuck in this old bag. And they no longer spoke the language. Now when I started to make The Four Seasons records the studio musicians didn’t speak the pop language. They had to be taught.

They didn’t want to overdub. They were used to doing the whole thing. They didn’t want to wear earphones. They couldn’t play with earphones. It was a lot – it was very, very different. Now here we come along and we’re sort of changing the face of the way that music was working. So I figured that there would come a time when I would not speak the language anymore. So after I had my run with Juice Newton and I had a couple of country hits in the ‘80s, I actually had my last chart record in the ‘90s. And when I left to come here to Florida it was ’92, I never thought that I would be able to write anymore

because the only business I knew was the record business. Little did I know, my wife was smart enough to know that I wasn’t going to stop writing, so she donated my services to the Pops orchestra and then I started to see the acts come in, they needed arrangements. And I’m saying to myself how come I didn’t know about this?
And now you’ve got a big band to write for.

Yeah. And well the orchestrations changed and a lot of things changed. But the other thing about the insecurity of not being current – every time you write an arrangement you’re showing up to the date naked. You’re letting it all hang out. You don’t know if they’re going to like it, they’re not going to like it, and there’s always something you know you did wrong. And it got to the point where I really didn’t have a good understanding about where I was as an arranger until many, many years later.
